Text:
Normal pulse rate in beats/min, by age group:

Neonate — {{c1::100 to 180}}

Infant — {{c1::100 to 160}}

Toddler — {{c1::90 to 150}}

Preschool age — {{c1::80 to 140}}

School age — {{c1::70 to 120}}

Adolescent through older adult — {{c1::60 to 100}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: age cuts both ways — a neonate's ceiling of 180 beats/min is baseline rather than distress, while an older adult gets no allowance at all and is held to the same 60 to 100 as a 20-year-old.

Cue: the lower bound walks down in clean tens — 100 for the neonate and infant, then 90, 80, 70, and 60 from adolescence on.

Text:
Normal respiratory rate in breaths/min, by age group:

Neonate — {{c1::30 to 60}}

Infant — {{c1::25 to 50}}

Toddler — {{c1::20 to 30}}

Preschool age — {{c1::20 to 25}}

School age — {{c1::15 to 20}}

Adolescent through older adult — {{c1::12 to 20}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: an infant breathing 40 breaths/min is normal, but the identical rate in an adult is double the adult ceiling of 20 — a respiratory rate means nothing until the patient's age is known.

Cue: a neonate's slowest normal breathing, 30 breaths/min, is still faster than an adult's fastest normal, 20 — the two bands never overlap.

Text:
Normal systolic blood pressure in mm Hg, by age group:

Neonate — {{c1::50 to 70}}

Infant — {{c1::70 to 95}}

Toddler and preschool age — {{c1::80 to 100}}

School age — {{c1::80 to 110}}

Adolescent — {{c1::90 to 110}}

Early, middle, and older adult — {{c1::90 to 130}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: systolic pressure is the only one of the four vital signs that climbs with age — a neonate's floor of 50 mm Hg is little more than half the adult floor of 90.

Pitfall: an adolescent reaches adult pulse and respiratory values but not adult pressure — the systolic ceiling holds at 110 until age 19, then rises to 130.

Text:
Normal body temperature by age group:

Neonate — {{c1::98°F to 100°F (37°C to 38°C)}}

Infant and toddler — {{c1::96.8°F to 99.6°F (36°C to 37.5°C)}}

Preschool age through older adult — {{c1::98.6°F (37°C)}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: temperature is the one vital sign with no steady climb or fall across the age groups — its own band for the first three years, then a fixed 98.6°F (37°C) from preschool age onward.

Cue: the neonate is the only group whose normal reaches 100°F (38°C), and the infant and toddler are the only ones whose normal dips below 98°F.

Text:
The nine life-span age groups and the ages each one covers:

Neonate — {{c1::birth to 1 month}}

Infant — {{c1::1 month to 1 year}}

Toddler — {{c1::1 to 3 years}}

Preschool age — {{c1::3 to 6 years}}

School age — {{c1::6 to 12 years}}

Adolescent — {{c1::12 to 18 years}}

Early adult — {{c1::19 to 40 years}}

Middle adult — {{c1::41 to 60 years}}

Older adult — {{c1::61 years and older}}
Back Extra:
Why: no other phase of life changes as fast as the first year, which is why those 12 months alone carry two names — neonate for the first month, infant for the remaining eleven.

Pitfall: the childhood bands share a boundary year, so one age can sit in two groups — a 12-year-old is both school age and adolescent — while the adult bands do not overlap, since adolescence ends at 18 and early adulthood starts at 19.

Text: As a person gets older, pulse rate and respiratory rate {{c1::decrease::increase or decrease}}, whereas systolic blood pressure tends to {{c1::increase::increase or decrease}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the climb has a ceiling — systolic pressure stops rising once it reaches 90 to 130 in early adulthood and is identical in middle and older adults, so a high reading in a 70-year-old is a finding, not an age effect.

Cue: the same 70 mm Hg that is an infant's healthy floor sits 20 mm Hg below the adult floor of 90 — which is exactly why the ranges have to be age-banded at all.

Text: A pulse of 140 beats/min is a {{c1::normal::normal or life-threatening}} finding in an infant, but the same rate in a 30-year-old adult signals a {{c1::life-threatening::normal or life-threatening}} condition.
Back Extra:
Why: 140 beats/min sits inside the infant's normal 100 to 160 but runs 40 beats/min past the adult ceiling of 100 — a vital sign has no meaning until the patient's age is known.

Pitfall: the trap runs both ways — a pulse of 70 beats/min is unremarkable in an adult but dangerously slow in a neonate, whose normal starts at 100.
verified_by: p683 prose, verbatim: "Finding a pulse rate of 140 beats/min ... is usually normal for an infant. However, for a 30-year-old adult, the same values would likely signal the presence of a life-threatening condition." Corroborated on the rendered plate figures/TABLE_7_1.png: infant pulse 100 to 160 (140 inside), adult pulse 60 to 100 (140 far outside), neonate pulse floor 100. The prose's companion figure of 60 breaths/min was REMOVED by the editor: TABLE 7-1 caps infant respirations at 50 and puts 60 only in the neonate band, so the book contradicts itself on that digit.
